Ajani, Nacatl Pariah: First-pick bomb — ALSA 1.4 and a 64.2% GIH say it, and the card earns it: two bodies for two mana that flip into a planeswalker whose 0 both rebuilds and, with any red permanent, machine-guns. Perfect in RW, fine anywhere white.
Razorgrass Ambush: Solid playable, free-roll floor: it's a white source when you don't need combat removal, so the 84.9% play rate is doing the work. The negative IWD is the combat-only restriction — it can't break a board stall or kill a ramp target. Fine mid-pick in any white deck.
Witch Enchanter: Solid white playable with no cost: the back face is a white land, so it's never a dead card, and the front is a 4-mana 2/2 that eats an equipment, umbra or Eldrazi enchantment. 86.8% play rate on a card that's half land tells the story — main it, don't first-pick it.
Hydroelectric Specimen: Role-player with a free floor. The 1/4 flash body walls Jeskai aggro and the redirect turns an opposing removal spell into a two-for-one, but it's reactive and the 53.4% is average. Real value is the land back: never a dead card in any blue deck.
Sink into Stupor: Free-roll playable: it's an Island that occasionally buys a turn against a bomb or a crewed vehicle. The 80.6% play rate is the whole story — you slot it as land #17 and cast it maybe a third of games. Never a high pick, never a cut.
Tamiyo, Inquisitive Student: First-pick mythic. A one-mana 0/3 flier walls the RW and RG aggro decks on turn one and still attacks for a Clue, and the flip is live in UB where the draw-three engine turns her sideways into a planeswalker. 66.5% opening-hand WR — she is best early, not a topdeck.
Boggart Trawler: Filler with a free roll. The 3/1 body trades down and the graveyard exile is blank outside UB Sneaky Snacker decks, but the land back means it never costs you a slot. Take it as a late black playable, not a pick you make early.
Fell the Profane: Premium removal with a free land stapled on — unconditional kill at instant speed, and the dead copies become a black source instead. The 3.1 ALSA and 89% play rate are correct; the double-black keeps it honest in three-colour wedge decks, so it's best in UB or straight-black builds.
Sorin of House Markov: Early pick, near-bomb. A two-mana 1/4 lifelink blanks the RW and RG aggro starts the format is built on, and extort plus the flip side turn a defensive body into inevitability. The +5.5 IWD is what a card that stabilizes and then wins looks like.
Pinnacle Monk: Solid playable with a free floor: the back half is a red land, so it never costs you a slot, and the front is a prowess body that rebuys your best burn. The five-mana 2/2 front is unexciting alone — 55.8% with negative IWD says it's played as a land that sometimes wins a long game, not as a threat. Take it mid in any red deck.
Ral, Monsoon Mage: Trap mythic — 50.6% GIH and negative IWD make him the worst-performing early pick in this chunk. A 1/3 body that needs a heavy instant/sorcery density MH3 doesn't reward, and the coin flip damages you on losses. Playable in UR, never the reason to be there.
Sundering Eruption: Role-player: you are drafting the land side. The negative IWD with an 81% play rate is the tell — it's a red source that occasionally blows up a landscape or forces through the last four damage in RW. Never a spell slot, always a free roll.
Bridgeworks Battle: Real removal that costs you nothing to maindeck — the back half is a Forest, so the 91.6% play rate is the MDFC floor and the 56.0% is the fight mode doing work. Not the C+ baseline other MDFCs get; take it as a green playable, high in GW/BG/RG.
Disciple of Freyalise: Playable as a land first, spell second. {3}{G}{G}{G} is only castable in a heavy-green Temur build, and sacrificing a 0/1 Spawn draws nothing — you want a real body. The 55.8% is largely the back face being a free untapped Forest; don't pick it as a payoff.
Grist, Voracious Larva: Good but not a format-warping mythic — 54.0% GIH is mediocre for a card taken at pick 2.6. As a 1-mana deathtouch blocker it's fine on rate; the flip condition (creatures entering from your graveyard) almost never comes up in MH3 Limited, so you're paying mythic priority for a Wall.
Bloodsoaked Insight: Play it as a land. Seven mana before reductions means the spell side only fires in a BR deck already winning the damage race, and the -0.3 IWD says drawing it changes nothing. 78% play rate is the tapland half doing the work, not the sorcery.
Drowner of Truth: Two cards in one and the reason 91.3% of blue decks run it: a tapped dual early, a 7/6 that makes two spawn late. LoL's "C+ tapped Island" undersells the GU ramp mode, where the colorless-spent trigger actually fires. Take it as fixing, cash it as a finisher.
Glasswing Grace: Play it, rarely prioritize it. Five mana for +2/+2 flying lifelink is a real game-ender on an evasive body, but it 2-for-1s you into removal and WB is the format's worst pair. The land back is why the 55.7% holds up: it is a free inclusion in any W or B deck.
Legion Leadership: Solid playable and effectively free — the Jeskai land back guarantees it makes the deck, which is why play rate is 89% on a middling trick. Doubling power plus first strike is a genuine blowout in RW go-wide combat; it wants a real board, so hold it for a decent board state.
Revitalizing Repast: Strong combat trick for one mana that also counts as a land — the counter is permanent, so it saves a creature and leaves it bigger, and it's a modification for Abzan. Take it in any BG/GW deck; the MDFC back means it never clogs.
Rush of Inspiration: Solid Jeskai playable with an MDFC floor — you always sleeve it in U/R as a free land. Note trap 5: the two energy is a bank withdrawal, so in a deck without spare energy this is a random-discard draw-two. Fine, never a high pick; don't let it talk you into UR, the format's biggest overrate.
Strength of the Harvest: Auto-include in GW, and the land back means it's never a dead card in any green or white deck. On a wide Abzan board it's a multi-counter pump that also triggers modified; on an empty board it's a Forest-Plains. 55.7% with flat IWD is exactly what a zero-risk flexible card looks like — good, not a first pick.
Stump Stomp: Solid playable that's never a dead card — 94.6% play rate because the land back half means you always run it. As removal it needs a fat body, so it's best in RG spawn/Eldrazi where Writhing Chrysalis and a spawn-fed beater turn it into a clean kill. Take it, don't force it.
Suppression Ray: Solid playable that doubles as fixing. Five mana to tap-all is only worth casting as an alpha-strike button in WU/RW energy, and the stun counters compete with energy you'd rather spend elsewhere. Most decks just run the land half — the +0.4 IWD says so.
Waterlogged Teachings: A UB dual that occasionally tutors your best instant. The 55.4% is mostly land, not spell — the tutor mode is four mana for zero board impact. Free inclusion in UB, which wants exactly this kind of untaxing dual, but never a real pick.
Breaker of Creation: The Temur (GU/RG) top end, not a reason to be Temur. Annihilator 2 plus hexproof-from-colors ends games, but {6}{C}{C} demands landscapes or Spawn as real colorless sources. OH 52.9% vs GD 57.0% says it's a card you want to draw late, and it rides decks that already had the ramp.
Devourer of Destiny: Premium Temur top end: the cast trigger exiles any colored permanent whether or not the 6/6 resolves, so it's removal stapled to a finisher. 56.6% GIH with a +4.0 IWD, but {5}{C}{C} means you need landscapes or spawns — take it in GU/RG with ramp, cut it elsewhere.
Drownyard Lurker: Solid Temur playable that is never stuck. Cycling for 2U early or a 7/7 vigilance plus a spawn late is exactly the flexibility the GU ramp deck wants, and it makes a colorless source for double-colorless costs. Mid-pack pick, not a priority.
Echoes of Eternity: Trap despite LoL calling it a bomb — 51.8% GIH and a negative IWD say it loses games you were winning. Six mana and triple-colorless means you need landscapes plus spawn just to cast it, and then it does nothing to the board. Only in an assembled Temur pile.
Eldrazi Ravager: Replaceable top end. Six mana for a 6/6 annihilator 1 is the payoff you are told not to prioritize — negative IWD confirms it does not carry games. Cycling {2} keeps it from being a mulligan, so run one in Temur and let the rest wheel; take the two-drop ramp instead.
Emrakul, the World Anew: Format-ending in the deck that can cast it, and the opening-hand-to-drawn gap (53.1% vs 61.3%) says exactly that — it's dead cardboard early and a concession later. Madness for six colorless means spawn tokens and landscapes actually get you there. First-pick it, then draft the RG/GU ramp to support it.
Glaring Fleshraker: A colorless-matters engine that ramps and drains: each colorless spell makes a spawn, and each colorless creature entering pings. Only really live in Temur (RG/GU) where colorless density is high, but there it's a real build-around body with 3.2 ALSA reflecting heavy demand.
Herigast, Erupting Nullkite: Weakest mythic here — 52.5% is replacement-level for a card you first-pick. Emerge at 6RR still asks you to sacrifice a body for a 6/6 flier, and the emerge-granting text is a Constructed line. Play it in red as a top-end flier; don't build toward it.
It That Heralds the End: The most important common for Temur Eldrazi — take it over the fatties, which wheel. Two mana that anthems your spawn and colorless drones while shaving a mana off the top end; LoL is right that multiples are fine. The 54.3% understates it because it's dead outside the wedge; inside GU/RG it's a first-pick-quality glue card.
Kozilek, the Broken Reality: Archetype-conditional payoff, not a slam. +4.6 IWD and a 9/9 anthem win games outright, but 56.0% is riding Temur decks that already had the ramp — doctrine says take the two-drop accelerants over the fatty. At ALSA 1.5 he's a first pick only if you're already GU/RG.
Kozilek's Command: First-pickable in Temur and a fine reason to prioritize colorless sources. 60% GIH with +7.1 IWD and a 2.4 ALSA is real: two modes at instant speed scales from a 2-mana exile plus spawn to a game-ender. The {C}{C} demands landscapes or spawns, not basics.
Null Elemental Blast: Sideboard card, and barely that — 6.8% play rate, sub-47% GIH. It answers only multicolored permanents and demands a true colorless source you likely spent on Eldrazi costs. Leave it in the pile unless you see a signpost gold uncommon across the table.
Nulldrifter: Premium blue rare because it is never a dead card: evoke for {2}{U} is a fine Divination on turn three, and the 7-mana mode is a flying Annihilator finisher. 94% play rate across every blue deck. Take it early; you cast it in Temur ramp and UB control alike.
Twisted Riddlekeeper: First-pickable blue uncommon and the reason to keep cheap chump bodies around. Ben's read is right — emerging on four for a 5/5 flier that stuns two blockers ends games. The gd_wr/oh_wr split (58.9 vs 52.2) is the tell: it's a mid-game haymaker, not an opener.
Ulamog, the Defiler: The format's biggest trap by pick position. ALSA 1.6 means it goes first-pick, yet 51.8% GIH and a dismal 48.7% opening-hand WR expose it: ten mana is castable only in assembled Temur ramp. Take the two-drop ramp instead and this wheels far later than people think.
Warped Tusker: Excellent Temur common because it is never dead: cycle for {2}{G} plus a spawn when you're flooded on top end, cast it as a 6/8 reach wall that also ramps. The modest +0.7 IWD reflects how often it's just a cycler — that flexibility is the value, not the body.
Wastescape Battlemage: High pick for the whole Temur wedge. A {1}{C} 2/2 that scales into a bounce spell or artifact/enchantment exile late is exactly the flexible early play the ramp decks want, and it pays you for the landscapes and spawns you already need. 58.0% with a strong drawn WR — always good.
Aerie Auxiliary: Premium white common and a first-pickable one. A 3/3 flier that hands out two +1/+1 counters is a clock plus a modified enabler, and the flat OH/GD split (59.2/59.0) proves it's a standalone good card, not a synergy payoff. Great in WU flyers and GW counters alike.
Ajani Fells the Godsire: Exile-a-fatty stapled to a token and a finisher — three chapters of value for five, and the 57.4% is honest. The +0.7 IWD says it's slow to matter when drawn late, so it's a strong midgame card for GW/WU rather than a tempo swing.
Argent Dais: Trap rare, essentially a sideboard card at 12% play. Two mana, then two more plus a tap to exile — and you hand the opponent two cards. Too slow for the aggro wedges and too symmetric for the grindy ones. Cut it.
Charitable Levy: Sideboard at best. Taxing your own noncreature spells for a delayed single card and a tapped Plains is a bad rate in a format that is aggro-or-go-over-the-top, and the 1.3% play rate with an 8.3 ALSA means nobody ever found a deck for it. No live WR because essentially nobody played it — don't be the one who does.
Dog Umbra: Role-player, and LoL's "C" is roughly right — the two modes are flexible but neither is strong. The 55.9% is mostly GW bestow/auras decks using umbra armor as counter-protection on a modified body; the pseudo-Pacifism mode is a tempo patch. Fine mid-pack filler, never an early pick.
Envoy of the Ancestors: Abzan filler. A 2/3 body with an outlast mana sink is fine on defense, but lifelink-on-modified only matters in a GW/BG board that already stuck counters, and the flat 54% with identical OH/GD says it neither wins early nor grinds late. Playable, never a signal.
Essence Reliquary: Trap. Three mana and a tap for a slow self-bounce does nothing to a board, and the −3.8 IWD is the tell: drawing it makes your deck worse. Only in a built aura deck rescuing enchanted creatures, and even GW has better threes.
Expel the Unworthy: Filler removal, and the data undercuts LoL's "cleanest white removal" read — 52.1% GIH with a negative IWD and only 48.5% play. The mv-3 cap misses the Eldrazi and the kicker costs five. Play it in a white deck, never take it over a real two-drop.
Flare of Fortitude: Sideboard. 15.6% play rate and 51.3% GIH — a free Fog-plus-protection only matters in a blowout combat or against a sweeper, and MH3 has almost no sweepers to blank. Negative IWD confirms it: drawing it does nothing. Leave it in the board.
Glyph Elemental: Premium white uncommon, take it over most removal. 58.4% with a 62.2% opening-hand WR is a pure curve card: play it turn two and it grows every land drop, and bestow rebuys it late. Ben's #1 white uncommon read is correct; it's the GW engine.
Guardian of the Forgotten: Filler body in GW/WB modified. A 4/4 vigilance for four is fine on rate, but the manifest trigger asks your counters-and-auras creatures to die, which is the opposite of what those decks want. Negative IWD confirms it's a body you play, not a payoff you build toward.
Guide of Souls: Pack-one-pick-one for Jeskai. It is the set's only truly repeating energy source outside Battle Wagon and Cartographer, and the {E}{E}{E} attack trigger converts a go-wide RW board into a flying three-counter kill. 67.5% GIH and a 72% opening-hand WR — the single best card in this chunk.
Hexgold Slith: Strong aggressive two-drop for Jeskai energy. The OH/GD split (58.7% vs 53.6%) is the tell: you want it on turn two to snowball counters, and it's a weak topdeck. Two energy on entry pays its own first-strike tax once — after that it's feeding off your bank.
Indebted Spirit: Role-player, not a priority. LoL's C+ read is right — a one-drop that trades up and leaves a flier, or a late bestow that gives a modified body afterlife. Fits aggressive GW and the weak WB pair; the negative IWD says play it early, never topdeck it.
Inspired Inventor: Playable glue, not a high pick. LoL's "best pivot card in the format" is a statement about flexibility — it slots into all three wedges — not power; 54.5% with a −2.2 IWD says a 2/2 for three whose mode rarely changes a game. Take it late, play it, move on.
Jolted Awake: Role-player in the Jeskai energy decks specifically, and only once your curve is settled. LoL's C+ is right: cycling {2} guarantees it's never dead, and with banked leftover energy it rebuys a four-drop for one mana. The −2.3 IWD confirms it's a late-deck filler you're happy to draw only when you already had the energy.
Mandibular Kite: Premium white common — 58.4% GIH with a 60.5% OH is the profile of a card you want in your opener, and one mana for a recurring flying body is the highest floor at the rarity. Ben's #3 white uncommon read holds: it feeds modified in Abzan and evasion in WU energy. Take it early.
Metastatic Evangel: High pick in any white aggro deck — take it over most commons. OH WR above GD WR marks it as a curve card, not a late topdeck: a 3/1 for two that quietly grows counters and, per Ben, refuels energy too. It's the cleanest RW/GW/WU pivot card in white.
Muster the Departed: The data corrects Ethan's B. 51.9% GIH at a 33.5% play rate means it's mediocre even where it gets played, and its home — WB modified/sacrifice — is the worst pair in the format. Needs creatures dying on your turn to do anything. Filler.
Nyxborn Unicorn: A GW role-player that's better as a 2/2 on turn two than as a five-mana aura. OH 55.6% above GD 54.2% confirms it's an early-drop card in the bestow/counters deck, which quietly finished 4th. Bestow is late-game insurance against blowouts, not the plan.
Ocelot Pride: The best card in this chunk and a first-pick over any removal: 65.5% GIH, 72.4% opening-hand, pick 1.7. Ethan's "how do you gain life" worry is answered by the Cat itself — lifelink means it triggers off its own attack. A one-mana mythic that snowballs unanswered.
Pearl-Ear, Imperial Advisor: Solid three-drop, not a bomb. A 3/4 lifelink for 1WW blanks Jeskai attackers on its own, which is most of the 55.2%; the aura-affinity and draw trigger only matter in a built GW auras deck. Draft it as a body, treat the text as upside.
Phelia, Exuberant Shepherd: Premium early pick for any white aggro deck — 60.1% GIH with a 63.3% opening-hand WR, meaning she wins by hitting the board on turn two and attacking. Flash plus the exile trigger removes a blocker, resets your own ETB, or eats an opposing token permanently. First-pickable in RW and GW.
Proud Pack-Rhino: Solid white playable that crosses wedges. A 3/3 for three with a shield counter is a modified enabler for Abzan and a counter-doubler for anything with proliferate value; LoL's "plays in multiple archetypes" read is right. The −0.5 IWD says it is a curve card, not a game-breaker.
Rosecot Knight: Filler at five mana — the 25% play rate is the honest verdict. A 3/4 vigilance body doesn't move a format this fast, and the dig only pays in artifact- or enchantment-heavy BR/GW builds. Last-slot material, cut it when your curve is full.
Solstice Zealot: Solid common for the Jeskai wedge — a 2/3 body that brings two energy and then converts leftover energy into repeatable tappers, which is real removal-adjacent value on a stalled board. The -1.5 IWD marks it as a curve card, but energy decks want the bank.
Static Prison: Premium removal in Jeskai (RW/WU), a liability outside it. One mana to exile anything, but the upkeep energy tax means the two it brings buys only a couple of turns unless you have a real bank — so take it high when energy-committed and treat it as temporary tempo when not.
Thraben Charm: Quietly one of the better white commons — 57.1% GIH on a 78% play rate. The kill mode scales with your board, so it's excellent in RW and GW go-wide and near-dead in a stalled or empty-board deck; the enchantment and graveyard modes are real sideboard relevance in a set full of build-around enchantments. Solid mid-pick removal.
Voltstorm Angel: Strong uncommon finisher for Jeskai — a 4/4 flier that brings three energy is a legitimate energy feeder by doctrine, not a spender. 56.6% understates it because the double-white pushes it toward RW/WU builds where the +1/+1 mode closes go-wide races. Early pick in white energy.
White Orchid Phantom: Solid but overrated on the land-destruction line — most of the time you're just giving an opponent an untapped basic to fix their splash. Buy the 2/2 flier with first strike for RW/WU energy, accept the WW, and note the −4.3 IWD: it's a curve-out card that's dead late.
Wing It: Playable trick, not a priority. The negative IWD (−2.2) with a 54.5% GIH is the aggro signature: fine in the RW/GW curve-out deck that's already attacking, dead weight anywhere reactive. Permanent flying counter also turns on modified in Abzan.
Wrath of the Skies: Archetype-conditional, and closer to a trap than LoL's "A" — with only four energy realistically available it usually kills your own board too. Numot's refill argument overrates it. Good in a slow WU/WB control shell, actively wrong in RW energy aggro, which is the deck white most wants to be.
Aether Spike: Strong Jeskai common that everyone underrates — pick 6.3 for 56.2% GIH is real value. It's a hard counter for two mana when you've banked energy, and it pays for itself by generating the two it spends. Best in WU/UR tempo where you're holding mana anyway.
Amphibian Downpour: Blue's best answer to a bomb and the one it can cast at flash speed. Stripping abilities down to a 1/1 handles Eldrazi and equipment carriers alike; the +3.1 IWD and 57.7% drawn WR reflect a card you hold for the right target. Leaves a blocker, so pair it with evasion.
Bespoke Battlewagon: Solid, not an engine to build a deck on. LoL called it the format's repeatable energy generator and rated UR "A" on it — UR finished 9th at 53.72%, and the Wagon's own 54.6% with a 62.2% play rate is the correction. Crew 4 is real. Play it in Jeskai; don't move into it.
Brainsurge: Take it high in UB, cut it elsewhere. Instant-speed draw four fuels the draw-three payoffs and refuels the control deck's grind, and the 72% play rate tells you it is a real archetype card, not a maindeck staple. Ethan's fetchland framing overrates it — UB is exactly the deck that should not play landscapes.
Consign to Memory: Sideboard card, not a maindeck one — the 16% play rate and sub-51% GIH overrule Numot's "always main-deckable." It's a blank against RW energy and BG modified; it's excellent against the Eldrazi wedge's cast triggers and the big colorless top end. Board it in on the play against Temur.
Copycrook: Archetype-conditional playable. Four mana for a copy of the best creature on board is fine when boards are good, embarrassing when they're not — hence the 49.6% opening-hand versus 55.0% drawn split. Play it in slower UB or WU decks that can see a target first.
Corrupted Shapeshifter: Filler at best — 49.2% and a 35% play rate mean most drafters correctly leave it in the sideboard. Four mana for a modal blocker or vanilla 3/3 flier does nothing in a format that wants you aggressive or ramping. 23rd card.
Deem Inferior: Premium blue common, and LoL's B+ is if anything low given UB finished 5th, not the C+ the hosts called the archetype. +4.0 IWD and a 5.6pp gap between opening-hand and drawn WR is the signature of a cost-reducer — it's a clunky four-drop in a vacuum and a one-mana answer to anything once your draw-three engine is online. Take it high in UB or WU.
Depth Defiler: Near-bomb uncommon: 59.7% GIH with +6.6 IWD, the best card-advantage rate here. Kicked it's a two-for-one bounce-plus-loot at instant speed off a 3/5 wall, and devoid plus a colorless kicker makes it a natural in GU Eldrazi as well as straight UB. First-pickable.
Dreamtide Whale: Two swings of 7 for three mana — a tempo finisher, not a value card. GD well above OH means it's best drawn into a stalled board where 14 damage ends it; on turn three it just eats a chump. Fine in UB or UR, weak if you can't attack.
Electrozoa: Ben's D+ is closer than Ethan's C. The 3/1 body is embarrassing; you're paying three mana to flash-block something and bank two energy. Marginal 23rd card in WU/UR energy, and only when you'll actually spend that energy elsewhere.
Emrakul's Messenger: Premium blue two-drop: an evasive clock that also manufactures colorless sources for double-{C} costs. +3.9 IWD and 85.6% play mean it's good without the draw-two trigger firing, and excellent in UB draw-three or blue Eldrazi. Take it over most commons.
Flare of Denial: Good in a blue deck, not a splash-magnet. 55.8% GIH with a 4.7pp gd/oh gap — it's a reactive card you want to draw, not open. The free mode (sac a blue creature) is a real trick against a bomb; otherwise it's a fine three-mana Counterspell in UB control.
Harbinger of the Seas: Sideboard card, essentially unplayable. A 2.1% play rate and no recorded GIH WR say it all: the static ability turns your own landscapes and MDFCs into Islands, wrecking the fixing a three-wedge format demands. Provisional read on thin data, but a 1UU 2/2 with a self-harming drawback is a pass.
Hope-Ender Coatl: Strong blue uncommon and a genuine tempo swing: flash in a 2/2 flier on their end step and the Force Spike trigger taxes whatever they're deploying. 57.6% GIH with +4.2 IWD across 87% of blue decks — it's good in WU flyers and UB control alike, no synergy required.
Kozilek's Unsealing: Archetype-conditional build-around, and a middling one. 52.7% with a 66% play rate means even the GU decks that ran it were not winning off it — it does nothing on an empty board and demands a real density of four-plus-drops. Late playable in dedicated Eldrazi ramp only.
Petrifying Meddler: Solid Temur common and the best defensive body blue offers. The cast trigger stuns even if the creature is countered or the Meddler is killed, buying a turn, and a 4/5 reach wall is what blue ramp needs to survive to its Eldrazi. Middling opening-hand WR — it's a stabilizer, not a curve card.
Roil Cartographer: One of the best blue two-drops in the set: a 1/3 that blocks the aggro decks, banks energy off every land, and turns into a draw-three with landscapes. 58.4% GIH and +4.9 IWD across an 80% play rate — this is a high pick in any energy or UB deck.
Sage of the Unknowable: Narrow role-player that matters more than 51.6% suggests: it is one of the few real colorless sources for double-colorless Eldrazi costs, and 0/4 walls off the RW starts while you ramp. Only in GU/RG Temur — dead weight anywhere else.
Serum Visionary: Premium common for any blue deck, no archetype tax. A 2/2 body that replaces itself and scries 2 at 58.7% GIH with +4.7 IWD — that combination of high win rate and high improvement means it's carrying games, not riding a built deck. It's the reason UB draw-three got there; prioritize it over most of blue's uncommons.
Shadow of the Second Sun: Powerful but slow — 58.4% with only a 62.7% play rate says the decks that ran it won, and plenty correctly cut it. Six mana for an extra untap/draw each turn is a pure grind engine, which fights MH3's "be aggressive or go over the top" axis. Play it in UB control, side it out against RW.
Strix Serenade: Trap — the 9.5% play rate is the verdict. Handing an aggressive format a 2/2 flier to Mana Leak a creature is a losing trade, and 43.8% GIH confirms it. Sideboard it against an Eldrazi deck and even then think twice.
Tamiyo Meets the Story Circle: Filler at best — 43.3% opening-hand vs 52.7% drawn is the widest split here, meaning it's a card you never want early. Chapter I stalls one attack, II loots into clues, III is rarely relevant. Slow value UB only.
Tempest Harvester: Energy feeder and looter — a legitimate Jeskai role-player, since it banks two energy and only spends one at a time. The 65% play rate is colour-restriction, not weakness. Fine in WU/UR; in a non-energy blue deck it's a 2/1 that filters. Mid-pick.
Triton Wavebreaker: Filler at best — 47.7% GIH and a 19.6% play rate say blue's bestow creature is a trap. A 1/1 prowess body or a +1/+1 aura both lose to any removal spell, and blue isn't the prowess color here. Last playable in a WU deck short on two-drops.
Tune the Narrative: Take it early in any Jeskai lane. A one-mana cantrip that banks two energy is the glue for RW, WU and UR — energy is a bank with only two repeatable sources, so a card that brings two and costs nothing in tempo is the enabler. Ethan's #1 blue common holds up.
Ugin's Binding: Premium blue pick at 60.4% GIH and +6.6 IWD. The floor — three-mana instant bounce — is playable everywhere; the graveyard mass-bounce is Temur-only gravy that almost ends the game when it fires. Take it in any blue deck and treat the recursion as a bonus you rarely need.
Unfathomable Truths: Best-in-class blue common for the value decks. Five mana at instant speed for three cards plus a spawn triggers the UB draw-three payoffs and supplies a colorless source for the Temur side. The 60.1% drawn WR is the tell: this is a card you want to draw, not mulligan into.
Utter Insignificance: Fine blue common removal, closer to Ethan's C than Ben's C-. Flash makes it a combat blowout and the 1/1 shell stops a fatty cold, but you need a real colorless source (landscape or spawn) to actually exile — otherwise a bounce or blink undoes it. Playable, never premium.
Volatile Stormdrake: A two-mana 3/2 flier that steals their best creature and banks four energy to keep it — you effectively pay the mana value out of the energy. Swingiest blue rare in the format at 58.3%; take it early and hold it for a real target rather than casting it on turn two.
Accursed Marauder: Strong black common and better than it reads: you can sacrifice the Marauder itself to its own trigger, making it a two-mana one-sided edict. +4.2 IWD confirms it. It gets worse against wide spawn boards (nontoken only), so prioritize it into the grindy pairs.
Arcbound Condor: Archetype-conditional and weaker than the note implies. Ben's #3 black uncommon read is too high: 52.1% GIH with a 50.8% opening-hand WR means a double-black four-drop 3/3 flyer that does nothing if you only have a couple of artifacts. In BR artifacts proper the −1/−1 triggers are a real engine. Outside it, a mediocre body — take only when committed.
Breathe Your Last: Premium black common and a removal benchmark — unconditional at instant speed is exactly what UB and Abzan want. The 53.2% OH versus 58.5% GD gap is the double-black tax showing up in openers; that's the real cost, so don't splash it and don't run landscapes over it in a UB deck.
Chthonian Nightmare: Good engine, not a bomb. The three energy is a one-time bank and the recursion needs both a body to sacrifice and a cheap creature worth rebuying, so it shines in BR artifacts or BG grind and does nothing in a flood. +4.4 IWD, 80% play — a real card, take it midpack.
Consuming Corruption: Solid removal with a real mana-base tax — X equals Swamps, so landscapes and splashes cut it down. That makes it a UB card specifically, the one deck the doctrine says should stay strictly two colours. There, +3.8 IWD and the life swing are genuinely good.
Crabomination: Bomb, and the best card you'll see in this chunk — 64.2% GIH and +12.5 IWD. A 5/5 for six that strips three zones and casts a free spell off the exile wins the game outright. Emerge off an artifact makes it cheap in BR. First-pick it out of any pack.
The Creation of Avacyn: Cut it. 46.5% GIH, 7.8% play rate — three mana and three turns to tutor one creature into play, while you lose life for the privilege. Far too slow for a format that is either aggressive or ramping past you. Unplayable outside a UB deck with nothing else to do.
Dreadmobile: The experts were wrong here; the data is brutal. LoL called it a top-two black uncommon and a premium early pick, but 50.3% GIH with a -2.5 IWD and 35% play rate says a crew-1 vehicle that needs artifacts to eat is a BR-artifacts-only card. Late pick outside that deck.
Dreamdrinker Vampire: Filler two-drop for the Abzan modified decks. Lifelink plus mana-sink adapt gives it late-game relevance, and the menace trigger turns it into a real clock once counters start landing. 53.8% at an ALSA of 6.2 — it wheels, so take the payoffs first.
Drossclaw: BR artifacts or bench it. The 7.2 ALSA and 42% play rate price it correctly — a living-weapon body that ticks up artifact count for Cranial Ram and Refurbished Familiar, and almost nothing outside that. If you have not seen Rams by pick four, this is not a reason to stay.
Emperor of Bones: Strong two-drop and a high pick. Adapt 2 makes it a mana sink that grows past removal on its own, and it's a natural fit in BG modified where counters come from everywhere. The reanimation is real upside rather than the plan — a 2/2 for two that takes over a stalled board is already the card.
Etched Slith: Filler. Menace on a 1/1 means the counters accrue only against empty or bad boards; the counter-removal rider is mostly a cute upside. 52.5% with a 50.8% drawn WR says it fails as a topdeck — a curve two-drop for BR artifacts or BG counters, nothing more.
Etherium Pteramander: Good aggressive one-drop for black decks, best in BR artifacts where the adapt cost actually shrinks into a real mana sink. Evasive from turn one with a late-game mode is exactly what a 55.7%/+3.0 profile means — a card with no dead draws. Solid mid-pick.
Eviscerator's Insight: Role-player, best when you have spawn tokens, afterlife bodies, or cheap artifacts to feed it. The +2.6 IWD and 5.5pp opening-hand-to-drawn gap say it's a card you want mid-game with a board, not in your seven. Flashback makes it a genuine grind card in UB and BR; don't play it in a deck with no expendable permanents.
Fetid Gargantua: Filler. 52.0% and a flat IWD — a five-mana 4/4 whose adapt-draw needs three more mana and costs life, which is too slow for a format this fast. Only playable as a top-end body in BG modified where a second counter source retriggers the draw. Late pick, first cut.
Flare of Malice: Premium removal in the Eldrazi era: killing the largest creature is exactly what you want against Temur top end, and the free-cast mode off a black creature blows out a bad block. Double black, and it whiffs on a wide board, but +4.3 IWD says it gets there.
Gravedig: Late playable. Neither mode is a card you want on turn two, and the 3B entwine is where it's actually good, so it's a five-drop pretending to be a two. 50.6% at 41.3% play — it's the 22nd card in a grindy black deck.
Grim Servant: Filler for heavy-black decks only. OH 49.4% against GD 55.4% is the whole story — it's terrible on curve when devotion is low and fine once you have a board, exactly LoL's "uncastable when behind" complaint. A 3/2 menace with a self-inflicted 3 life is a 22nd card.
Kami of Jealous Thirst: Exactly the UB draw-three payoff LoL said didn't exist at common — 56.2% GIH, and the 6.8pp gd/oh gap marks it as a synergy card, not an opener. Deathtouch blocks the whole format on turn three; the free drain closes games once you're actually drawing three. Good in UB, filler elsewhere.
Lethal Throwdown: Premium one-mana removal in the right shell. A format full of Eldrazi Spawn and living-weapon tokens makes the additional cost close to free, and sacrificing a modified creature replaces itself. Ethan's B- is the right read over Ben's C; the +2.2 IWD confirms it kills real cards.
Marionette Apprentice: Premium uncommon that transcends its archetype: 60.5% GIH and +7.1 IWD in a WB pair that finished dead last. Any chump-blocked token, sacrificed spawn, or afterlife body drains, so it converts a stalled board into a clock from nowhere. Ethan's "Splinter Twin" framing with spawn tokens is right — take it over most removal.
Mindless Conscription: Strong in UB, unplayable outside it. A recurring amass 3 every turn you hit three draws is a genuine win condition, but the 57% play rate shows how narrow the trigger is. The 58.9% is conditioned on the draw-three deck existing — do not take it as a speculative pick.
Necrodominance: Trap. Triple-black on a do-nothing enchantment that costs you your draw step, caps your hand at five, and does nothing to a board — 44.3% GIH and a 13% play rate agree. There is no Limited deck that wants this. Leave it in the sideboard.
Nethergoyf: Excellent one-drop in any black deck — it grows on its own without support and recurs from the yard late, which is why the +6.1 IWD is the highest-tempo mark on this list. Not a bomb, but a first-pickable mythic that makes UB and BR curves work at both ends.
Quest for the Necropolis: Filler you cut. Six mana minus counters to reanimate one creature, as a sorcery, in a format that punishes doing nothing on turn one. Sub-50% GIH and a 36% play rate; leave it for the BG grind decks that already have too many slow cards.
Refurbished Familiar: Format-defining black common, exactly as LoL says — take it high in BR and it's still fine in a base-black deck at four mana. 56.9% with +3.9 IWD on a 2/1 flier that strips a card; in artifacts it lands turn two and just wins tempo races. One of the few cards that rewards the BR lane without requiring it to be assembled.
Retrofitted Transmogrant: Useful one-drop role-player, not a priority. 54.7% with +1.9 IWD comes from the two decks it actually serves: BR artifacts needs the artifact count, and BG modified likes a recursive body that comes back with two counters already on it. Fine at pick 6, wrong at pick 2.
Ripples of Undeath: Unplayable. 5% play rate and 43.3% GIH: paying mana and life every turn for a card you may not want, while milling yourself, is not a plan any deck in this format wants. Leave it in the sideboard.
Scurrilous Sentry: Quietly one of black's better commons: menace plus connive on entry and every attack means it filters, grows, and gets through. +4.0 IWD at 56.7% with no build-around needed. Fine in UB draw-three (fuels graveyard) and BR alike.
Shilgengar, Sire of Famine: Take it for the 6/6 flier for five; the Blood-sacrifice reanimation almost never assembles in a 40-card game. OH 51.7% vs GD 57.1% flags a card that's clunky in your opener but dominates once cast. {B}{B} in a WB shell — the format's worst pair — caps it below its rare-slot look.
Warren Soultrader: Overrated rare — pick 3.7 for a 51.8% GIH is a loss. A 3-mana 3/3 is on rate, but MH3 has no sacrifice payoff wedge worth building around, and paying life plus a creature for a Treasure is a bad trade in a format this aggressive. Play it as a body.
Wither and Bloom: The best black common and a top-five removal spell in the set. -3/-3 at instant speed answers the whole aggro curve, and the graveyard mode makes it live again in the grind — a +5.2 IWD is enormous for a two-mana common. First-pickable in any black lane.
Wurmcoil Larva: Strong black uncommon and a wall aggro cannot profitably attack into — deathtouch-lifelink that replaces itself with two more bodies. 56.8% GIH with +4.3 IWD; the artifact type is a real bonus for BR Cranial Ram counts. Solid mid-pick in any black deck.
Aether Revolt: Weakest kind of energy rare. The ping only fires when you gain energy, and energy is a bank with two repeatable sources — you will trigger this three or four times a game, not every turn. Negative IWD at 54.3%. Playable RW filler, never a first pick.
Amped Raptor: Slam — the best red uncommon and one of the best cards in the format at 64.2% GIH. First strike for two is already fine in RW, and the cascade-off-energy trigger regularly converts the two energy it just made into a free spell. Ben's #1 red uncommon read is exactly right; take it over most rares.
Ashling, Flame Dancer: Trap. Four mana for a 4/4 is fine, but the magecraft payoff needs two or three instants/sorceries in a single turn — no MH3 deck reliably does that. 51.6% with a negative IWD confirms it plays as a vanilla body; take real red cards ahead of it.
Detective's Phoenix: High pick and one of red's best rares — 93.6% play rate, 58.8% GIH. It's a three-mana hasty flier that, once your graveyard is stocked, keeps coming back for {R} to turn any body into an evasive threat. The recursion is the card; the front half is just the down payment.
Eldrazi Linebreaker: Bomb-adjacent rare and one of the best cards in RG — 2.2 ALSA says the table agrees. A three-mana 3/3 trampler that hands out haste and a scaling pump every combat converts a wide spawn board into lethal out of nowhere. 58.5% with +4.1 IWD; the {C} pip means you need landscapes or spawn, which the deck already wants.
Fanged Flames: Premium red common, second only to Galvanic Discharge — deal 4 with exile answers almost everything at a price the aggressive decks can pay, and devoid means it feeds Eldrazi count in RG. 91% play rate and ALSA 3.5 say it never wheels. Ethan's #2 red common read is correct.
Flare of Duplication: Not a Limited card — 9% play rate. Copying a spell requires you to have a spell worth copying plus a red creature to eat, and the 45.5% GIH shows what happens when people try. Last pick.
Frogmyr Enforcer: Trap outside a built BR artifact deck, and shaky inside one. Prototype 2/2 for 3R is below rate and the 4/4 needs a board of artifacts you don't have — −4.3 IWD, 26.8% play. If you're relying on this, you didn't get the Rams.
Furnace Hellkite: Trap outside a committed BR artifact deck. Only 31 artifacts exist in the set, so affinity rarely shaves more than one or two — a 50.9% GIH and 46% play rate are what a seven-mana dragon in practice looks like. If you don't have Cranial Rams, you don't have this.
Galvanic Discharge: The format's removal benchmark and the best common — take it over anything short of a bomb. 60.1% GIH with a 92.9% play rate and near-identical OH/GD splits means it's always good, never conditional. It kills on any curve point and banks the energy your Jeskai deck spends elsewhere.
Ghostfire Slice: Premium red removal, second only to Galvanic Discharge. Four damage covers everything the fair decks play, devoid dodges color hate, and in a three-wedge format with gold signposts everywhere the cost reduction fires often enough to make it a one-mana instant. 92% play rate, ALSA 2.9 — it never wheels.
Glimpse the Impossible: Good red common conditioned on the deck: the 57.7% GIH with only +1.3 IWD and a 59.3% drawn-WR says this is a mid-game card that rewards a low curve or spawn payoffs. In RG it's three mana for cards plus ramp; in a clunky deck you exile lands and get nothing.
Infernal Captor: Near-last playable. Four mana for a 3/3 plus a Threaten only pays when you have a spawn or germ token to exploit, and even the RG spawn decks mostly passed — 29% play rate, 7.7 ALSA, negative IWD. Take it as a 23rd card in a sacrifice-heavy red deck.
Inventor's Axe: Role-player for RW energy. It brings its own two energy for the first attach, but every re-equip drains a bank the format barely refills — treat it as a one-shot +2/+0 with flash. The 33% play rate is right: playable filler and a modified enabler, never an early pick.
Mogg Mob: Sideboard-adjacent. {R}{R}{R} is a real cost in a three-colour wedge format and the 14% play rate says nearly everyone cut it, but as a 3/3 that converts into three damage split however you like it's fine in a mono-red-leaning aggro build. Not a pick you make on purpose.
Molten Gatekeeper: Go-wide payoff, not a standalone card — the −1.8 IWD against a 54.3% GIH is the signature of a deck card. In RG spawns or RW tokens each creature is a drain trigger and unearth gives a free extra one; in a fair deck it's a 2/3 that does nothing. Prioritize only once your token engine exists.
Party Thrasher: First-pick-quality red rare that needs nothing — a two-mana 1/4 blocks the format's aggro starts while generating a card of selection every turn, and the convoke clause makes the exiled spells castable off your board. 58.5% GIH with a 60.1% opening-hand WR is the profile of a card you always want turn two. Take it over most red commons.
Phyrexian Ironworks: Skip it. 52.5% with −2.0 IWD is one of the worst energy cards in the set: it spends three energy to do something once, and doctrine's rule is energy is a bank with only two repeatable sources. It also needs you to already be attacking. Sideboard in a grindy RW deck at best.
Powerbalance: Unplayable, provisional read — no GIH sample and a 3.6% play rate. Hitting on mana-value parity off the top is a coin flip you can't build around in a 40-card deck, and it does nothing to the board in a format where you must be aggressive or go over the top.
Ral and the Implicit Maze: Take it high in any red deck — 58.6% at a 77.8% play rate with ALSA 4.4 beats both LoL grades. Chapter I is one of only two sweepers in the set and is often one-sided against the go-wide RW/RG boards, then II and III keep paying.
Reckless Pyrosurfer: Premium RW common-slot uncommon and a core piece of the best deck. OH 58.0% over GD 55.2% marks it as a curve card you want in the opener. Battle cry off every landscape turns a go-wide board into lethal — Ethan came around for good reason. Take it over most removal in RW.
Reiterating Bolt: Premium red uncommon, second only to Discharge in the color. Three damage for two answers most of the format's creatures, and the replicate line gives your leftover energy a real mana sink late. Sorcery speed and the -0.6 IWD are the only knocks; still an early pick in any red deck.
Sarpadian Simulacrum: Filler with a specific job. A one-mana hasty artifact body is a cheap Cranial Ram count and a crew enabler for BR, and the four-mana sac mode is real removal late. But 42% play rate and ALSA 7.2 mean you take this last and only in the artifact deck.
Siege Smash: Sideboard card, and the 55.2% GIH is a mirage — a 34.4% play rate and −1.9 IWD mean it only appears when someone maindecked it against BR artifacts. Split second on a Naturalize is cute, and the pump mode keeps it from being blank. Last-pick it, board it in.
Skittering Precursor: Good RG common-slot uncommon. A 3/3 menace for three is above rate in a format this aggressive, and the spawn trigger off landscape sacrifices and living weapon is real incremental ramp. 55.0% is the honest number for a solid beater, not a build-around — take it mid-pack.
Skoa, Embermage: Playable top-end for a committed red deck — deal 4 stapled to a 4/4 is real value, but six mana with RR is a lot in a format that ends around turn eight. Take it mid-pack as a curve-topper for RW or BR, and cut it if you already have two six-drops.
Smelted Chargebug: Take it as a top-tier red common — LoL has it as Ben's #3 and the numbers agree: a menace body that survives combat, banks two energy for your real payoffs, and pushes damage through. Plays in RW and BR alike; the 5.5 ALSA means it often tables past where it should.
Spawn-Gang Commander: Top red uncommon and a first-pickable card in the format's second-best pair. Five mana for four bodies, two colorless mana of ramp, and a repeatable damage outlet that converts spare spawns into reach. Ethan's #2 red uncommon read is right — the 61.1% drawn WR is the go-wide plan cashing out.
Thriving Skyclaw: Overrated by the note. LoL's B treats it as "3/2 flier plus 3 energy," but the four-mana double-red body dies to everything and the pump costs all three energy — and energy is a bank with only two repeatable sources. 53.3% with −1.8 IWD and a 49.5% play rate: a fine RW filler, not the energy feeder its listing suggests.
Unstable Amulet: Underrated energy uncommon — 57.5% with a flat OH/GD split means it's good whenever you draw it, not a build-around. Two energy on entry plus a repeatable impulse-draw outlet makes it the rare card that banks and spends usefully. Solid mid-pick in RW or UR; don't expect the ping to matter.
Voidpouncer: Filler two-drop for RG/RW. A 3/1 for two trades down into everything, so the value is the late-game kicker into a 5/3 trample haste — but that needs a real colorless source, which basics can't provide. −2.1 IWD, 66% play: playable, never a priority.
Wheel of Potential: Trap, and the 8.2% play rate says everyone figured that out. Energy is a bank with only two repeatable sources, so you're rarely paying enough to matter, and the refill is symmetric — you're spending three mana to restock the aggro deck beating you.
Basking Broodscale: One of green's best commons and a Temur staple at 92.8% play. It's a two-drop that blocks, grows, and prints real colorless sources for your double-{C} Eldrazi — the mana-fixing half is the reason to take it early, not the 3/3 body. Wheels far less often than the fatties it enables.
Birthing Ritual: Trap mythic. 51.1% GIH and a 21.4% play rate — two mana that does nothing the turn it lands, then asks you to sacrifice a creature every end step in a format where boards get raced. You need a deep creature curve and time; MH3 gives you neither.
Collective Resistance: Main-deckable green instant, better than it looks. MH3 is dense with Eldrazi build-around enchantments, equipment and artifacts, so mode one or two is live most games, and the protection mode blanks removal in a tempo race. 57.8% at a 73% play rate means it's earning its slot, not sideboarding in.
Colossal Dreadmask: Top-end filler for green. Living weapon means six mana always buys a 6/6 trample even with an empty board, and both LoL hosts are right that it forces awkward answers. But −0.6 IWD says it's slow — fine in GU ramp, too expensive for the aggressive wedges.
Eladamri, Korvecdal: Pick order says bomb, results say playable. Drafters took him at 1.7 and got 53.5% with a +0.2 IWD — in Limited he is a 3/3 for three that occasionally cheats a creature in. Fine green three-drop; do not pass real removal or ramp for him.
Eldrazi Repurposer: Early pick and the glue of the Temur deck — Ethan's #1 green common, correctly. Two spawn from one card is ramp, chump blockers, and colorless mana for double-C costs, all on a 3/3 body. Nearly 60% GIH with a 92% play rate: it's good even when the Eldrazi plan doesn't fully come together.
Evolution Witness: Grindy glue for BG modified, exactly as the doctrine says — adapt turns it into a 4/3 that rebuys a permanent, which is a two-for-one in a long game. The 52.2% opening-hand versus 55.9% drawn gap says it's a midgame value card, not a curve play. Solid, not a priority.
Fanatic of Rhonas: The best card in this batch and a green slam — 60.5% GIH with a 64.8% opening-hand WR, meaning it's an on-curve accelerant, not a topdeck. Turn-two ramp into Temur's top end, a 1/4 that walls the aggro decks, and it eternalizes into a 4/4 later. Take it over almost anything green.
Fangs of Kalonia: Filler in GW/BG modified, and the weakest kind — a conditional pump that's blank without a creature and gets you two-for-oned. 51.7% with a 49.5% opening-hand WR is a card you'd rather not draw early. The overload at six is a real late-game finisher on a wide board, which is the only reason it makes decks. Late pick.
Flare of Cultivation: Near-unplayable at 50.3% and a 42.2% play rate. In a format where landscapes already fix and the Eldrazi plan wants bodies, sacrificing a green creature for two basics is a losing trade — the free mode costs you your board. Only a fixing patch for a greedy Temur splash.
Fowl Strike: Narrow removal saved by the reinforce mode. It's dead against Temur ground decks and excellent against WU flyers, and the 7.2 ALSA means you can wheel it and board it in. In an Abzan counters deck the discard mode makes it a fine 23rd card.
Gift of the Viper: Good cheap trick: one mana to untap and give deathtouch+reach blows out an attack or ambushes anything, and the counters make the creature modified for Abzan. 55.7% at 56.9% play. Not a priority pick, but a fine 20th card in GW/BG.
Horrific Assault: Premium removal — 58.9% GIH is top-of-format for a common, and Ben's surprise at making it his #1 green card was correct. One mana to eat anything with a big Spawn-fed body, plus 3 life in the Eldrazi deck. Take it near the top of any RG/GU pack.
The Hunger Tide Rises: Filler, and only in a deck built for it. 49.8% GIH with a -3.1 IWD: three mana for three 1/1s across three turns is too slow to stabilize and too small to attack. The chapter IV tutor wants a sacrifice payoff the format doesn't offer. Play it in BG/GW only if short on bodies.
Hydra Trainer: Trap. A 1/1 for two that must exert to pump and costs three more to grow itself is too slow for a format that wants pressure or a top end, and -3.2 IWD is one of the worst marks in green. The 64% play rate is drafters over-trusting the counters theme; it does not pay.
Lion Umbra: Near-trap outside a built GW auras deck: 52.0% GIH and a 40% play rate, because "enchant modified creature" means you need a counter or equipment already on board before this is castable. Umbra armor blunts the two-for-one, but the setup requirement is real. Low pick.
Malevolent Rumble: Premium green common — take it over most uncommons. Two mana that digs four deep for the enchantment or fatty, fills the yard, and leaves a spawn behind is the perfect turn two in any green deck. 60.4% with a 60.8% opening-hand WR: it is good early and late, in Temur especially.
Monstrous Vortex: Trap. Four mana that does nothing on arrival and demands power-5 creatures you'd rather just cast — 46.2% GIH with an 8.6% play rate is the whole story. Ben's initial B was a dry read of the ceiling; in practice the GU ramp deck wants ramp, not a lottery ticket. Don't play it.
Nightshade Dryad: Near-rare-quality green common and the pick both experts flagged: a deathtouch blocker that fixes any colour and produces the colorless your Eldrazi costs demand. 58.7% with a 61.6% opening-hand WR — that's mana acceleration doing work. Take it over most uncommons in Temur.
Nyxborn Hydra: Strong green common that never sits dead: a scalable body early and a bestow pump later, so removal can't two-for-one you. Best in GW auras/counters, fine in any green curve. 86.5% play rate — this is a core playable, not a build-around.
Path of Annihilation: Take it very high in Temur — 61.1% GIH with +7.1 IWD and a 2.9 ALSA is elite. It fixes the whole wedge (spawn tap for any color, Eldrazi tap for any color), makes two bodies on entry, and buys back your life total when the fatties land. LoL's B undersells it; this is the card that makes GU ramp actually function.
Primal Prayers: Worst card in the chunk and a hard pass — 40.7% GIH, −6.8 IWD, 4.6% play rate. Four mana that does nothing on arrival, then cheats out only three-drops using an energy bank with almost no refills. Exactly the build-around-with-no-engine trap the doctrine warns about.
Propagator Drone: Take it high in RG — the data (56.4% GIH, 91% play, 2.7 ALSA) is well ahead of LoL's C+/C read. A two-drop that turns spawn chaff into growing bodies and becomes a mana sink when the game goes long is exactly the Eldrazi go-wide deck's engine piece.
Signature Slam: Premium green removal — ALSA 3.1 and 90.7% play at 59.2% GIH, and Ben's "Clearshot with upside" undersells it: every modified creature piles on, so in a GW/BG board it kills anything. Take it over most creatures in the Abzan wedge.
Six: Strong green rare. The 2/4 reach body stonewalls the aggro decks on turn three, then retrace turns every excess land into a rebuy of your best permanent. 59.0% GIH with +5.2 IWD — it's good early and great late, which is rare. Early pick in any green deck.
Sowing Mycospawn: First-pickable green rare and the ramp piece the Temur deck actually needs — it finds a landscape or a colorless land, so it fixes the double-colorless problem while adding a body. 59.1% GIH, +6.0 IWD, pick 2.1. Kicker to strip a land is upside; the tutor is the card.
Springheart Nantuko: First-pick green rare. Two mana, bestow to protect it, and every land after that copies your best creature — a 59.1% GIH with +5.8 IWD and ALSA 1.6 is the profile of a card that wins the game by itself. Landscapes double the trigger count. Slam it.
Temperamental Oozewagg: Honest green common — a 4/4 for four with a mana sink that makes it a 6/6, plus a trample anthem that matters in Abzan. 54.4% GIH on a 76.7% play rate is exactly what a solid body-first common looks like. Mid-pick; never exciting, never a mistake.
Territory Culler: Real green beater, not a clunky Eldrazi. A 7/5 reach for five brutalizes the RW flyers deck and blanks ground attacks immediately, and the landfall dig means late copies still convert to gas. 92.5% play rate at 56.7% — this is a top-two green uncommon in ramp or midrange.
Thief of Existence: Overdrafted — ALSA 2.6 on a 51.6% card. The exile trigger whiffs constantly because MH3 decks run few cheap noncreature permanents, and when it hits you hand back a card. What you're really paying a hard colorless pip for is a 3/4. Fine Temur body, low priority.
Trickster's Elk: Marginal. A 3/3 for three is below rate here, and bestow that erases abilities is a liability as often as an upgrade — you turn your own modified creature into a vanilla Elk. 51.5% and a -3.0 IWD; last playable in GW, cut it when the deck has better threes.
Wumpus Aberration: Take it high in Temur. Four mana for a 6/6 trample is over the format's rate curve, and the drawback is empty often enough — and fully avoidable once you can spend {C} from a spawn or landscape. ALSA 3.0 says it never wheels; the RG/GU decks know.
Abstruse Appropriation: Premium removal, and better than its 56.6% looks — +5.7 IWD with a 3.0 ALSA means it's an instant-speed unconditional exile that also steals the thing. WB is the worst pair in the format, which drags the number; the devoid text lets you cast the exiled card off colorless mana, so it's playable anywhere you have both pips. First-pick it in white-black.
Arna Kennerüd, Skycaptain: Bomb where castable, but the WUB cost is the whole problem — 55.4% with +5.4 IWD on only a 66.3% play rate means it sat in a third of the pools that opened it. A 4/4 flying lifelink ward body wins on its own; the counter-doubling is gravy for WB/BG modified. Take it and build toward it, don't splash it.
Conduit Goblin: Premium common for the best deck in the format. A 2/2 for two that banks two energy and converts a single energy into a haste attack is pure RW curve material — the 60.8% OH WR is the giveaway that you want it in your opener, not as a late pickup.
Cranial Ram: The BR artifact deck's backbone and the doctrine's bail-out test — if you haven't seen a Ram by pick four, abandon the archetype. The 56.0% is conditioned on that deck existing; living weapon means it's never blank, but in a non-artifact deck it's a 1/1.
Cursed Wombat: The Wombat is real; BG is not. LoL's "A" and "strongest uncommon" call is half-right — counter-doubling on every adapt creature is genuinely busted, but the archetype finished 8th at 53.72% and the card's own 54.9% reflects that. Take it if you're already BG; don't move into BG for it.
Cyclops Superconductor: Fine UR common, not a reason to be UR — remember the data corrects LoL here, UR finished 9th. 54.4% GIH at pick 7.0 makes it a solid late body: a 2/2 prowess that brings three energy and threatens a death-trigger Shock if you haven't spent it. Energy discipline makes this card.
Emissary of Soulfire: Role-player and a legitimate energy battery. Three energy on ETB behind a 1/4 that blocks the format's aggro is the real card; the exalted mode is anti-synergy in a WU deck that wants to go wide with flyers. 54.1% and 58% play rate say playable signpost, not a reason to be WU.
Expanding Ooze: Weak gold common, and a warning sign: 51.4% GIH with negative IWD. LoL rated BG modified "A" on Cursed Wombat, but the pair finished 8th, and this is why — a 3/3 for three whose attack trigger needs a *second* modified creature to do anything. Play it as a body only.
Faithful Watchdog: Best GW common on rate. Two mana for a 3/3 vigilance beats every two-drop in the format and arrives pre-modified for the Abzan payoffs and bestow/auras. GW quietly finished fourth at 56.48%; the 58.6% opening-hand WR says play it on curve, always.
Genku, Future Shaper: Solid WU rare and a real build-around anchor. The 2/5 body walls the RW aggro decks that dominate the format, the token trigger turns every removal spell or dying creature into value, and the five-mana pump is a board-wide finisher. Not a bomb — it needs your other permanents dying to shine.
Golden-Tail Trainer: Avoid. The worst-performing card on this list at 47.7% with a -6.6 IWD and only 40% play rate — a 1/3 whose cost reduction and anthem both scale off its own power of 1. GW is a good archetype; this signpost is not the reason, so don't read it as an open signal.
Horrid Shadowspinner: Very good in UB, unplayable outside it — the 54.3% play rate at ALSA 6.3 means only UB drafters take it, and they win with it (+5.7 IWD). A lifelinking 2/3 that fuels the draw-three/graveyard shell every attack. LoL's C+ read on UB was wrong; the pair finished 5th, and this is part of why.
Imskir Iron-Eater: Trap. An eight-mana body that needs a critical mass of artifacts to be castable at all, in a set with only 31 artifacts — 47.3% GIH, 44.5% from the opening hand, and −5.0 IWD make it one of the worst rares to first-pick. Even a fully assembled BR deck is better served by a Cranial Ram. Play it only as a genuine BR top-end after the deck exists.
Invert Polarity: Conditional but strong — +5.2 IWD and 56.3% GIH mean a coin flip between "counter it" and "steal it" is still fine, because the floor is a hard counter for three. UUR is genuinely restrictive, which is why the play rate sits at 62.7%. A real card in UR energy tempo, nothing outside it.
Izzet Generatorium: Trap tied to the format's biggest expert overrate. Paying four energy per card in a set with only two repeatable sources means you're spending the bank to draw, not to win, and 49.4% GIH with 36% play is the result. UR energy tempo finished 9th — don't build toward this.
Kudo, King Among Bears: Anti-synergy trap in its own colours. Setting everything to 2/2 wipes out the +1/+1 counters and bestow that GW is built on, and it only shines against Temur's fatties. −2.1 IWD, 36.4% play; the 53.2% is people sideboarding it correctly.
Nadu, Winged Wisdom: Bomb. A 3/4 flier for three would be a fine card with no text; the trigger then turns every combat trick, adapt activation, or aura into free cards and free lands. 60.6% GIH and +8.2 IWD across 87% of GU decks. P1P1 it and build Temur around it.
The Necrobloom: Skip it. 46.9% GIH, 30.2% play rate, and it's WBG — three colors for a 2/7 that makes 0/1s. Seven differently-named lands is not happening in a 17-land deck, so you get chump blockers and a dredge ability you don't want. Splashing three pips for this is how you lose.
Obstinate Gargoyle: Filler in the format's worst pair. Persist on a 2/2 gives WB two bodies out of one card, but flying needs a modification you may not have, and 50.8% with a 31% play rate confirms it. Only playable if you're already deep in WB modified artifacts.
Ondu Knotmaster: Sideboard-adjacent at 50.1% GIH, the worst number in this group, in the format's worst pair. The creature half wants a graveyard full of modified creatures you were happy to lose; the spell half distributing two counters is the mode you'll actually cast. Take WB payoffs elsewhere.
Phlage, Titan of Fire's Fury: First pick over almost anything. Three mana for Lightning Helix plus a 6/6 attached, and escape means removal only buys the opponent a turn. 64.9% GIH with a 65.6% drawn WR — it wins from anywhere, and RW is already the best pair in the format.
Planar Genesis: Role-player that smooths the Temur mana. Digging four for a landscape or a colorless source is exactly what a GU ramp deck with double-C costs needs, and it never rots in hand — it can always grab a spell instead. Middling WR because it doesn't affect the board; take it mid-pack, not early.
Psychic Frog: First-pick bomb and the best card on this list — 62.3% GIH with a 67.2% opening-hand WR and +11.2 IWD, numbers that only come from a two-mana threat that draws cards, grows on demand, and flies over. Take it and commit to UB, which the experts underrated at C+ and finished 5th.
Pyretic Rebirth: BR-only role-player, not a reason to be BR. Four mana for a card back plus damage is a fine instant-speed two-for-one, and affinity's inflated mana values do let it kill big — but 52.8% and a 49.2% opening-hand WR say it's clunky in multiples. Play it when the artifact deck is real; don't speculate on it.
Riddle Gate Gargoyle: The best common in WU and the premium energy two-drop — a two-mana 2/2 flier that banks 3 energy passes the vanilla test before the lifelink text matters. 58.4% with a 58.9% opening-hand WR says you want it turn two, every time. The 6.3 ALSA and 59% play rate are the gold-pip discount, not a quality signal: it wheels more than it should.
Rosheen, Roaring Prophet: Trap rare — a 9.4% play rate is the verdict, and the 52.6% comes from that tiny sample. MH3 has almost no X spells worth ramping into, so you're paying four mana for a vanilla 4/4 with a mill-six that usually whiffs. Playable body in RG only if you're short on four-drops.
Scurry of Gremlins: Near-bomb uncommon and a top-3 pick in RW. Two bodies plus a pile of energy plus a repeatable team pump and haste is a one-card alpha strike; 60.8% GIH with +3.3 IWD and a 3.9 ALSA means it converts a board into lethal, not just value.
Snapping Voidcraw: The GU ramp piece that matters more than it looks: it taps for two real colorless, which is how you actually pay double-colorless Eldrazi costs, and it blocks early. 78.7% play at ALSA 4.5. Take it over any big Eldrazi — those wheel, this doesn't.
Sneaky Snacker: Excellent in UB, unplayable elsewhere — 59.3% GIH with a 6.8 ALSA and only 57.9% play means it's a late-wheeling card whose number is conditioned on the draw-three deck existing. A recurring evasive body is exactly what UB grind wants, and LoL's "C+" on that archetype was badly wrong.
Titans' Vanguard: Near-bomb in RG and the payoff that makes spawn tokens lethal — the cast trigger fires even if it's countered, and every attack pumps the whole colorless board. 59.2% GIH at pick 2.8. Ben's Overrun comparison is right; just make sure your creatures are actually devoid/spawn first.
Wight of the Reliquary: Strong two-drop that gets better as the game goes long. It fixes and ramps off spare spawn tokens and grows past everything once creatures start dying — +4.7 IWD is the tell. The ceiling is high but BG modified finished 8th, so it's a good card in a mediocre lane, not a reason to force it.
Writhing Chrysalis: The best common in RG and a first-pick: 64.1% GIH with +9.1 IWD is bomb territory for a common. Four mana buys three bodies plus two colorless sources for your double-colorless costs, and it grows every time you crack a spawn. Numot's signal read holds — seeing it late means Eldrazi is contested.
Disruptor Flute: Do not maindeck. A 0.4% play rate with no win-rate sample is the format's verdict: naming a card in a 40-card singleton pool taxes one spell you may never see. Sideboard curiosity against a known bomb, nothing more.
Idol of False Gods: Marginal — a 50% card that only makes sense in a dedicated spawn deck. Two mana up front then {1}{C} per token is slow for a format this fast, and annihilator 2 at eight counters is a card you will never see. Playable ramp filler in GR/GU, cut otherwise.
Solar Transformer: Resolve the split toward Ben: this is premium, because it ramps, fixes all five colours, and banks three energy in one card. The colorless it makes is exactly what double-colorless Eldrazi costs need, so it's live in both Jeskai energy and Temur ramp — a rare genuine wedge-crosser.
Vexing Bauble: Never play it. A 7.1% play rate is the whole review — the counter clause is a Constructed hate card and nothing in MH3 Limited casts free spells. Cycling it for a card at two total mana is not a Limited deck slot.
Winter Moon: Unplayable in Limited — 0.4% play rate, no live WR. A two-mana artifact that taxes nonbasic untaps does essentially nothing here: the format's nonbasics are sacrifice-lands and tapped duals, so it hits neither player meaningfully. Provisional read from the text only, but there's no deck. Leave it in the pack.
Archway of Innovation: Do not play it. 44.5% with −2.6 IWD and a 10.4% play rate — a land that can enter tapped and whose improvise ability needs an artifact deck that lives in BR, not blue. There is no UB/UR artifact deck in this format for it to serve. Cut it from every pool.
Arena of Glory: Free-roll land for a heavily red deck. 55.9% GIH is mostly the decks it lives in, not the card — it fixes nothing and the exert cost is real, so only run it when you're base-red and can afford a land that sometimes enters tapped. Low priority, fine inclusion.
Bloodstained Mire: Not a landscape — it only finds a basic Swamp or Mountain, so it's fixing with none of the landfall/energy/spawn triple-duty that makes the DFC lands premium. Fine free inclusion in BR, a slot-filler elsewhere. 54.4% is mostly "played by two-colour BR decks."
Bountiful Landscape: Take it high in Temur — landscapes are triple-duty here: fixing, a real colorless source for double-{C} Eldrazi, plus landfall and Spawn triggers. 88.3% play at 56.6% GIH for a land is a strong signal. Only the cycling cost is a dead mode; you're playing it as a land.
Contaminated Landscape: Take landscapes early — this one does four jobs: fixing, a colorless source for double-colorless costs, landfall/shuffle triggers, and a cycling outlet. 55.4% GIH at pick 6.3 is a steal. The exception is UB control, which wants strictly two colors and hates the tapped-fetch tempo loss.
Deceptive Landscape: Take it higher than a land feels. Fixing for the Abzan wedge, a real colorless source for double-colorless costs, plus landfall and shuffle triggers, and cycling when you're already set. Baseline C+ that quietly enables three-color builds — never first-pick it, always play it in WBG.
Flooded Strand: Low-priority fixing, not a spell. Unlike the landscapes it adds no colorless source and no spawn, so it's a WU-only mana smoother with a +0.1 IWD — literally win-rate neutral. Take it late, run it if you're in Azorius, never over a playable.
Foreboding Landscape: Take landscapes higher than they feel. This fixes three colors, turns on double-colorless costs, feeds Skittering Precursor's sac trigger and shuffles for Brainsurge — triple duty for a land slot. 83.7% play rate at 55.6%. The one deck that should pass it is strictly-two-color UB.
Monumental Henge: Near-free inclusion in a heavily white deck, not a pick you spend on. It taps for W with almost no cost in a Plains-dense mana base and the four-mana dig gives late-game reach, but historic cards are scarce enough that the activation often whiffs. Low priority; the 43% play rate is about right.
Perilous Landscape: Take landscapes high, as the doctrine says — fixing plus a real colorless source plus landfall and shuffle triggers, with cycling as the late-game out. 56.2% is understated because it's mostly a land; the 5.7 ALSA is a mistake the table makes, so grab it ahead of marginal playables.
Polluted Delta: A land, and a below-market one outside UB. It fixes exactly the UB pair, which is the one deck the doctrine says should stay strictly two colours — so it fits, but it's a basic that costs a life. The real upside is shuffling for Brain Surge. Low priority; never over a playable.
Seething Landscape: Take landscapes high — they're triple-duty: fixing, a colorless source for double-colorless Eldrazi costs, plus landfall/shuffle synergies. 55.7% with +1.8 IWD on a land is genuinely strong. The exception is UB draw-three, which wants to be strictly two colors and can't afford the tapped, colorless-only turn. Great in Grixis-adjacent artifact or splash builds.
Shattered Landscape: Playable filler but the wrong landscape for this format — it fetches Mountain/Plains/Swamp, which spans no actual archetype: Jeskai wants blue, Abzan wants green. 54.9% is the baseline for "free fixing plus a colorless source," and the colorless tap is its best use for double-colorless costs.
Sheltering Landscape: Take landscapes high — this one is triple-duty: Naya fixing for RW or RG, a colorless source for kicker and Eldrazi costs, and a shuffle effect. 86% play rate and a 5.5 ALSA means it goes later than it should. Grab it over marginal playables.
Shifting Woodland: Effectively an untapped Forest with a mode you'll turn on once a draft — 2GG for a copy of a graveyard permanent needs delirium, which green Limited decks rarely assemble. 75.7% play at 55.2% is the free-land effect. Always play it; never pick it early.
Snow-Covered Wastes: Effectively a non-card at 11.5% play. It's a colorless-only basic, so it fixes nothing and costs you a coloured source. The narrow case is an extremely heavy Eldrazi deck short on landscapes needing one more {C}; even then prefer a landscape. Leave it in the sideboard.
Spymaster's Vault: Excellent in any black deck — a near-free land slot that turns into card selection plus counters once bodies start trading. 57.0% GIH and +4.0 IWD off a land is strong. The Swamp condition is trivial in BR/UB/BG; skip it only if black is a light splash.
Tranquil Landscape: Solid free inclusion, slightly ahead of its Abzan sibling at 55.5% and an 81.5% play rate. It fixes GW and GU simultaneously, banks a landfall trigger for Glyph Elemental or Springheart Nantuko, and supplies colorless for Eldrazi costs. Mid-pack pick, auto-play in any green deck.
Twisted Landscape: Take it high in Jund-ish and Temur decks — landscapes are triple-duty here: fixing, a real colorless source for double-colorless Eldrazi costs, and a cycling outlet when you're flooded. The 84.3% play rate and 55.5% GIH understate it because it's mostly a land. Prioritize over marginal playables.
Ugin's Labyrinth: Temur-only land. Untapped colorless is already worth something for the double-{C} costs, and imprinting a seven-drop turns it into a Sol Land that gives the card back. The +3.7 IWD is strong but the 59% play rate is the honest frame: it is a build-around land, not a free include.
Urza's Cave: Narrow fixer. It's a colorless source that can convert into a landscape, which matters in the Temur decks paying double-colorless — but it enters as a Wastes in a deck that also needs coloured pips, and 49.1% GIH reflects that. Play it only when your double-C count demands it.
Windswept Heath: A fetch land with no cycling mode and no colorless production, so it's just fixing plus Roil Cartographer/Brain Surge triggers in GW. The 54.4% play rate is the honest read — it's a free inclusion in the two colours it touches and a blank everywhere else. Never a real pick.
Wooded Foothills: Take it only as fixing for RG, the format's #2 pair, where it also turns on landfall. 55.5% GIH is the RG decks' WR bleeding through, not the land's power. It's a Mountain or Forest that costs one life — pick it after every real spell.
Angel of the Ruins: Playable top-end that mostly sits in your sideboard-adjacent slot — seven mana is a lot in a format that's aggro-or-Eldrazi, and 52.4% with a 50.4% opening-hand WR shows the cost. Plainscycling for {2} is the real value: it's never a dead card in a white deck. Take it late, play it as a one-of finisher with artifact/enchantment answers stapled on.
Decree of Justice: Marginal at 52.0% with a 31.3% play rate. Cycling for {2}{W} plus X soldiers gives it a floor, but the real mode costs six mana for two 4/4 fliers, which is a turn too slow for RW energy and a bad fit for anything else. Late playable in a grindy white deck only.
Distinguished Conjurer: Weak filler. A 1/2 that gains incidental life is below the bar in a format this fast, and the five-mana blink is too expensive to be the payoff. 49.6% GIH and a 46% play rate — only playable in a GW deck with real ETB creatures to reuse.
Orim's Chant: Unplayable in this format — 5.0% play rate and no win-rate data at all. One mana to Time Walk an opponent does nothing to a board, and MH3 punishes blank turns. Provisional read from the card itself: leave it in the sideboard.
Recruiter of the Guard: Solid playable whose ceiling is set by your pool — the 1/1 body is irrelevant, so you're paying three mana to tutor a toughness-2 creature. In GW/RW that's a Pyrosurfer or Broodscale, which is fine, not a bomb. 56.9% GIH, 69% play: a good white three-drop, not a first pick.
Sevinne's Reclamation: Solid white rare, not a bomb. 55.8% GIH at pick 3.5 — rebuying a two- or three-drop is fair value, and flashback means it's two cards in a grindy game. The +0.8 IWD is the honest number: it's card advantage, not tempo, so it's worse in the RW races white usually wants to be in.
Deep Analysis: Genuinely good in UB, and the experts underrated the deck it lives in. Four cards across two casts for a total of 4U and three life is exactly what the draw-three control pair wants, and the 58.6% drawn WR versus 52.9% opening-hand confirms it's a late-game card. LoL's C+ on UB was wrong; this is a high pick there.
Estrid's Invocation: Unplayable — a 6.9% play rate and 49.2% GIH. Three mana to copy an enchantment you already control assumes your deck has an enchantment worth copying, which in MH3 Limited means the GU Eldrazi build-arounds and nothing else. Cut it.
Kappa Cannoneer: Archetype-conditional finisher. Improvise plus ward {4} makes it an unkillable, unblockable snowball in a real artifact deck — but at six mana off raw lands in a blue deck with four artifacts it is a slow 4/4. The +4.4 IWD comes from the BR/UB artifact builds that actually cast it cheap.
Reef Worm: Grindy filler that rewards patience. A 0/1 for four is embarrassing on rate but the 3/3-6/6-9/9 chain makes it near-impossible to profitably attack through, which fits the UB control deck's stall plan. IWD +3.4 with a 51% play rate says it's a fine 22nd card, never a priority.
Shrieking Drake: Do not play it. A 1/1 flier that bounces one of your own creatures is card disadvantage without an ETB engine, and MH3 has no loop to abuse. 48.1% with a 44.0% opening-hand WR and a 13% play rate — the table is right to leave it in the sideboard.
Buried Alive: Unplayable. A 4.2% play rate and ALSA 8.3 mean it tables every single time: MH3 has no reanimation payoff worth building around at common, so this is three mana to do literally nothing to the board. Skip.
K'rrik, Son of Yawgmoth: Trap rare — the worst card in this chunk. 43.5% GIH, 38.9% from the opening hand, and a 21.7% play rate: a seven-mana 2/2 lifelink that you can only cast early by paying six life, in a format fast enough to punish exactly that. The mana discount doesn't matter when your black spells are two- and three-drops. Don't play it.
Nadier's Nightblade: Cut it. 46.9% GIH with −3.7 IWD is bottom-tier — a 1/3 for three that needs a dedicated token-sacrifice engine WB never really assembles, in the format's worst pair. Eldrazi Spawn would enable it, but that's Temur and this is black. Sideboard.
Ophiomancer: Effectively a bomb at uncommon-speed pricing — 59.7% GIH, +7.8 IWD, 2.1 ALSA and a 91% play rate is one of the strongest profiles in the set. A replacing deathtouch blocker every upkeep single-handedly stops Eldrazi ground assaults and enables sacrifice decks. Take it over most removal.
Toxic Deluge: Premium rare and a genuine format-warper — ALSA 2.3, 89.1% play, +6.3 IWD, and LoL's A is right. Scalable to be one-sided, which matters because the two best decks (RW, RG) go wide. Take it over almost anything except a two-drop bomb.
Victimize: Sideboard-to-filler. OH 46.7% against GD 53.9% is a card that needs a fodder creature and two dead bodies before it does anything — a terrible opener. In a Spawn deck the sac cost is free, but three mana sorcery-speed reanimation is too slow for a format that wants aggression or ramp.
Cursed Mirror: Underperformer at 49.0% GIH and 33.1% play rate.
